implementation_notes: Python has no inlining - the interpreter executes bytecode at runtime and cannot inline a Python function at all. The costs this pattern removes (call overhead, argument marshalling) are therefore a permanent feature of CPython, and the countermeasure is different: make the hot code C (a C extension, Cython, or a JIT like numba, or the vectorised operations in numpy which move the loop out of Python entirely). The Python-level levers are therefore (1) keep the hot loop in numpy or in C, (2) reduce the number of bytecode operations per iteration, (3) avoid attribute lookups in a loop by hoisting them to locals. Copying a Python function body into a loop to 'avoid the call' is occasionally done and does help a little (it removes the frame), but it duplicates the logic and is far less effective than moving the loop out of Python. In CPython 3.11+ the specialising interpreter (adaptive/specialising) already inlines many small operations at the bytecode level, so hand-inlining a Python function body gains much less than it used to.
idiom_name: no inlining in CPython; move hot loops to C/Cython/numba/numpy, or reduce bytecode ops per iteration
code_sketch:
# Python has no inlining; the frame per call is permanent. The lever is to
# move the hot work out of the interpreter entirely.
import numpy as np

def sum_np(xs: np.ndarray) -> float:
    return float(xs.sum())          # the loop runs in C, not in bytecode

# if it must stay in Python, reduce bytecode ops per iteration and hoist
# attribute lookups (the specialising interpreter in 3.11+ already does much
# of this, so hand-inlining a function body gains little):
def sum_py(xs):
    total = 0
    for x in xs: total += x          # a plain loop of BINARY_OP is the fastest form
    return total

# a C extension via Cython, or numba's @njit, inlines the whole function to
# machine code at import time:
pitfalls: There is no inlining in CPython, so an inline keyword or a copy of the body is a workaround, not a solution - the frame per call is inherent.
Manually copying a function body into a loop duplicates logic and only saves a frame; moving the loop to numpy/C/numba saves orders of magnitude more.
An attribute lookup per iteration (obj.attr) is a real cost that hoisting to a local removes - this is the Python analogue of what inlining enables elsewhere.
Cython's @cython.inline or cdef functions, and numba's @njit, compile the whole function to machine code at import time - that is the real inlining story for Python.
alternative: Move the hot loop into a C extension, Cython, numba, or vectorised numpy operations; on CPython 3.11+ rely on the specialising interpreter rather than hand-inlining
